HCC-CTX-G1.title: Lumora Care customer support policy (agent KB)
HCC-CTX-G1.text:
Lumora Care - Customer Support Policy (Agent Knowledge Base, revision 7)
Applies to Lumora Hub thermostats, Lumora Sense room sensors and the Lumora Plus subscription.

1. Identity verification
Before discussing account details, changing anything on the account, or issuing money, verify the caller with TWO of the following: the account email address, the last four digits of the card on file, the Hub serial number (starts with LH-), or a one-time code sent to the phone on file. A caller who cannot pass two checks may only receive general information. Never read out the full email, the address or any card digits to the caller; ask them to state it. An account holder may add one authorised user. Authorised users can troubleshoot but cannot cancel, request refunds or change billing details.

2. Hardware refunds
Hardware bought directly from lumora.example can be returned within 45 days of delivery for a full refund, in any condition, as long as the Hub serial matches the order. After 45 days there is no refund; the device is covered by the 2-year limited warranty (replacement, not refund). Purchases from retail stores must be returned to the store; we cannot refund those. Refunds go back to the original payment method only and take 5 to 10 business days after the warehouse scans the return. A prepaid return label is emailed within 1 business day of approval.

3. Lumora Plus subscription
Plus costs $6.99 per month or $69 per year. Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time and stay active until the end of the paid month; there are no partial-month refunds. Annual plans cancelled within 14 days of the charge get a full refund; after 14 days the plan runs to the end of its term with no pro-rated refund. Cancelling Plus does not stop the thermostat working; it removes energy reports, 90-day history and geofencing.

4. Duplicate and incorrect charges
If a customer reports two identical charges, first check the Billing tab. A charge marked "pending authorization" usually drops off within 3 business days and is not a duplicate. If both charges show "settled", the agent can reverse the duplicate directly with reason code DUP-01; the customer sees the money in 5 to 10 business days. Do not ask the customer to dispute the charge with their bank.

5. Goodwill credits
Tier 1 agents may issue one goodwill credit of up to $15 per account per 12 months, applied to the Plus balance. Anything larger, or a second credit within 12 months, requires a Tier 2 supervisor. Credits are never paid out as cash.

6. Outages
Confirmed service outages are posted on status.lumora.example. During an outage the Hub keeps running its last schedule locally; only the app and remote control are affected. Plus subscribers affected by an outage longer than 24 hours receive an automatic one-month credit; they do not need to request it. Do not promise a restoration time unless the status page shows one.

7. Shipping
Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days; express takes 1 to 2 business days and costs $12. If tracking shows delivered but the customer has nothing, ask them to wait 48 hours and check with neighbours, then open a carrier trace (form CT-2). We reship only after the trace closes, usually within 7 business days.

8. Escalation
Escalate to Tier 2 when the customer asks for a supervisor twice, when a refund or credit is above your limit, when there is a safety concern (burning smell, heat or sparks: tell the customer to switch the breaker off first), or when the customer makes a legal threat. Supervisor callbacks happen within 1 business day. Live transfers to a supervisor are not possible after 8 pm Eastern.

9. Privacy requests
Customers may request a copy of their data or deletion of their account. Agents do not process these on the call: send the customer to lumora.example/privacy, where the request is verified and completed within 30 days. Never confirm whether another person has a Lumora account.

10. Agents must not
Promise delivery dates, promise that a bug will be fixed by a date, offer discounts on hardware, share internal ticket notes, or comment on unreleased products.

HCC-CTX-G2.title: Lumora Hub troubleshooting guide for agents
HCC-CTX-G2.text:
Lumora Hub Troubleshooting Guide for Agents (version 4.2)
Use this guide on calls about the Lumora Hub thermostat (model LH-2) and the Lumora app. Always confirm the model on the Hub's back plate and the firmware version in the app (Settings > Device > About). Current firmware is 4.2.1.

A. Hub shows "Offline" in the app
1. Ask whether the Hub screen is on. A blank screen is a power problem: go to section C.
2. If the screen is on, have the customer open Settings > Network on the Hub itself. If it lists the home network but says "No internet", the problem is upstream: restart the router and wait 3 minutes.
3. The Hub only connects to 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Many mesh routers merge 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz under one network name; if the customer recently changed routers, this is the most likely cause. Ask them to enable a separate 2.4 GHz network or the router's "IoT" or "legacy devices" mode, then reconnect the Hub from Settings > Network.
4. If it is still offline, have them press and hold the Hub's dial for 10 seconds to restart it. A restart keeps schedules.
5. Do NOT suggest a factory reset (dial held for 30 seconds) unless steps 1 to 4 have failed and a Tier 2 agent agrees, because a factory reset erases schedules and removes the Hub from the account; the customer then has to set it up again from scratch.

B. Error codes on the Hub screen
E-14: lost contact with a Lumora Sense sensor. Replace the sensor's CR2032 battery; re-pair it from the app if needed.
E-22: the C-wire is not supplying steady power, so the Hub may restart repeatedly. Common in older homes. The fix is a C-wire or the Lumora Power Adapter. Agents must not guide the customer through wiring at the furnace or air handler; recommend a licensed installer.
E-31: temperature reading out of range. Usually the Hub is mounted near a heat source (a lamp, a sunny window, an oven wall). If the location is fine, treat it as a hardware fault and start a warranty replacement.
E-40: firmware update failed. Restart the Hub; the update retries automatically overnight.

C. Screen blank or flickering
Check the breaker for the heating and cooling system. If the customer reports a burning smell, heat or sparks, tell them to switch off that breaker, stop troubleshooting, and escalate as a safety case.

D. App login problems
- "Invalid credentials": have the customer use the app's "Forgot password" link. Reset links expire after 30 minutes and only the most recent link works.
- Reset email not arriving: ask them to check spam, and ask them to spell the email they are typing so you can compare it with the account. Agents cannot set a password for the customer and cannot read out the account email.
- Two-step code not arriving: codes go to the phone on file. If the customer no longer has that phone, the agent cannot change the phone number on the call; the customer must complete the Account Recovery form, which takes 2 to 3 business days.
- "Account locked": happens after 5 failed sign-in attempts and unlocks automatically after 15 minutes.

E. Schedule not being followed
Check whether "Eco Away" (geofencing, Plus only) is on and whether a household member's phone is still reporting "away". Also check for a manual hold: turning the dial sets a hold until the next scheduled change by default.

F. Known issue LUM-5561
Some Android 15 phones show the Hub as offline in the app even though it is working. Workaround: turn off battery optimisation for the Lumora app. Engineering has not published a fix date; do not give one.

HCC-CTX-C1.title: Lumora refunds and credits quick sheet (old printout)
HCC-CTX-C1.text:
Lumora Refunds and Credits - Quick Sheet (printed copy, no date on it)

Hardware returns
Customers can get a full refund on a Hub bought from our website within 30 days of purchase. Returns must be in the original packaging with all accessories included, or the return is refused at the warehouse.

Lumora Plus
Annual Plus can be cancelled at any time and we refund the unused months, pro-rated. Monthly Plus can be cancelled any time; no partial-month refund.

Goodwill credits
Tier 1 agents can apply a goodwill credit of up to $25 without approval. Use it when a customer has had a rough experience.

Outages
When the service is down, Plus customers get a one-month credit, and it's automatic.

Refund timing
Card refunds usually show up within 3 business days.

Common questions from agents

"What if the customer is just outside the return window?"
The return window is 45 days from delivery, so check the delivery scan, not the order date. Condition doesn't matter; we accept returns in any condition as long as the serial matches.

"Can I give a credit without a supervisor?"
All credits, of any amount, need supervisor sign-off recorded in the notes before you apply them.

"How do outage credits work?"
The customer must call within 7 days of the outage to claim the credit. We cannot apply it after that.

"Can annual Plus be refunded?"
Annual plans are refundable only within 14 days of the charge. After that the plan runs to term.

"The customer wants the money back faster."
Card refunds take 5 to 10 business days after the warehouse scans the item. We cannot speed this up.

HGEN-CTX-G1.title: Community garden plot holder handbook
HGEN-CTX-G1.text:
Maple Street Community Garden - Plot Holder Handbook

Welcome to Maple Street Community Garden. This handbook covers what every plot holder agrees to when they accept a plot. Please keep it somewhere you can find it; most questions we get during the season are answered here.

Fees
The annual plot fee is $45 for a standard 10 x 12 foot bed. Households that qualify for the city's utility assistance program pay a reduced fee of $20. Fees are due before you receive the shed code. Fees are not refunded after June 1, but if you give up your plot before then we refund half.

Getting started
New plot holders must attend one orientation. This season there are two: Saturday, May 16 at 10 am and Wednesday, May 20 at 6:30 pm, both at the tool shed by the north gate. Orientation takes about 45 minutes and covers the water system, compost bins, and the shed.

Your plot must be cleared of weeds and planted within 21 days of the date you are assigned it. If a plot is still bare after 21 days, the garden coordinator will send one reminder email. If nothing has changed seven days after the reminder, the plot is offered to the next household on the waiting list. We do this because the waiting list is currently 38 households long.

Workdays
Every plot holder contributes six hours of shared work per season. The easiest way is to come to our monthly workdays, held on the first Saturday of each month from 9 am to noon. Hours can also be earned by turning the compost, mowing the paths, or helping at the fall harvest swap. Log your hours on the clipboard inside the shed door. Plot holders who have logged fewer than three hours by August 1 will get a friendly check-in; we would rather help you find hours than lose you.

Watering
Water only before 9 am or after 6 pm. Midday watering wastes water and scorches leaves, and the city meter reads us as a single household. Hoses must be coiled back on their reels after use. Please do not leave sprinklers running unattended.

Being away
If you will be away for more than a week during the growing season, arrange a plot buddy to water and harvest for you, and let the coordinator know who it is. Absences longer than three weeks require written notice to the coordinator in advance, so we do not mistake your plot for an abandoned one. You can find a plot buddy through the garden group chat or ask the coordinator to match you with someone.

Growing rules
No synthetic pesticides or herbicides anywhere in the garden. Plants may not grow taller than six feet or shade a neighboring plot. Invasive plants such as mint must be grown in a container sunk into the bed. Diseased plant material goes in the black bin by the gate, never in the compost.

The shed
The shed code changes on the first of every month and is sent by text to all paid plot holders. Tools are shared; please clean them and hang them back where you found them. Personal tools can be stored in the labeled cubbies but the garden is not responsible for them.

Contact
Garden coordinator: Dana Whitfield, coordinator@maplestreetgarden.org. Dana checks email on weekday evenings. For anything urgent at the garden, such as a burst pipe, call the city parks line posted on the shed door.

Brightwater Studio - Move to the Harlow Building: Staff FAQ

We are moving from our current office on Fenwick Road to floors 3 and 4 of the Harlow Building, 220 Quay Street. This FAQ collects the answers to what people have asked so far. It will be updated as details are confirmed; the version date is at the bottom.

When is the move?
The last working day at Fenwick Road is Friday 13 November. The movers come over that weekend. The Harlow Building opens for us on Monday 16 November. Please work from home on Friday 13 November if you can; the office will be open but noisy and partly packed.

What do I need to pack, and by when?
Everyone gets two labelled crates. Put anything you want moved to your new desk into your crates and leave them at your desk by Thursday 12 November at 4 pm. Crates are collected after 4 pm that day. Anything left loose on or under a desk after that will be treated as unwanted and cleared. Plants are welcome but must travel in a crate or go home with you.

What about my monitor, dock and chair?
Company monitors, docks and keyboards stay where they are. Do not unplug them; IT will label and move all company equipment and set it up at the new desks before Monday. Personal equipment, including personal second monitors, footrests and chairs you bought yourself, must be taken home by Friday 13 November. The movers are not insured to carry personal items.

Do I have an assigned desk at Harlow?
For the first two weeks, desks are assigned by team and there is a seating plan on the wiki, so no booking needed. From Monday 30 November we switch to booked desks using the Deskly app. Each team keeps a home zone, but individual desks are booked daily.

Is there parking?
There is no free staff parking at the Harlow Building. The studio will subsidise monthly permits at the Canal Street garage, which works out to $60/month for staff after the subsidy. Permits are limited to 25 spaces and are allocated first come, first served. Apply through the People team form by Friday 6 November. There is a covered, secure bike cage on the ground floor with 40 spaces and showers on floor 3.

What happens to the kitchen and fridge?
The Fenwick Road fridge will be emptied and cleaned on Wednesday 11 November. Anything left inside at 5 pm that day will be thrown away. The new kitchen on floor 4 has two fridges, a dishwasher and a coffee machine.

What about post and deliveries?
From Monday 16 November, use 220 Quay Street as the delivery address. Post sent to Fenwick Road will be forwarded for three months. Personal online orders should not be delivered to the office during move week.

Who do I ask?
Questions about desks and equipment go to IT at the helpdesk channel. Questions about parking, access cards and the seating plan go to Tomasz Lindgren in the People team. Access cards for Harlow will be handed out at the front desk on Monday 16 November from 8:30 am; bring your current card to exchange.

Feed the starter once a day if it lives on the counter, once a week if it lives in the fridge. Equal weights of flour and water, about 50 grams each, and keep roughly 50 grams of the old starter. Rye flour makes it lively; plain white flour makes it milder.

It is ready to use when it has doubled within six to eight hours and a spoonful floats in water. If it smells like nail polish remover it is hungry, not dead. Pour off any grey liquid on top and feed it.

For a basic loaf: 100 grams active starter, 375 grams water, 500 grams bread flour, 10 grams salt. Mix everything but the salt, rest an hour, add salt, then do four sets of stretch and folds thirty minutes apart. Let it rise until it has grown by about half, shape it, and put it in the fridge overnight. Bake in a covered pot at 250 C for 20 minutes, then uncovered at 230 C for about 25 more.

Ruth's note in the margin: do not open the oven to peek, and do not cut it warm, no matter who is asking.

HLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Lecture 9 slides: Price Discrimination
HLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Lecture 9: Price Discrimination
Instructor: Prof. Dalia Ferreira-Stone. Slides v2, posted after class.

1. Why firms price discriminate
- A single-price monopolist leaves consumer surplus on the table and creates deadweight loss (DWL).
- Three conditions must all hold: market power, a way to sort buyers (or let them sort themselves), and no resale (arbitrage blocked).
- Prof's phrase for the third condition: "the resale wall." If the resale wall comes down, every scheme collapses back to a single price, because low-price buyers resell to high-price buyers until the prices meet.

2. The three degrees (course convention - use these labels on exams)
- First degree (perfect): each unit is sold at that buyer's reservation price. Consumer surplus = 0, output equals the competitive quantity, DWL = 0.
- Second degree: the price depends on the quantity or version bought (block pricing, bundles, "good / better / best" tiers). Buyers self-select from one menu that is offered to everyone.
- Third degree: different prices to observably different groups (students, seniors, regions). Rule: set MR in each market equal to the common MC. The group with less elastic demand pays the higher price.

3. Worked example (Slide 14) - the Lakeview Ferry
- Tourist demand: P = 120 - 2Q. Commuter demand: P = 60 - Q.
- MC = 20 for both groups; no fixed cost in this example.
- Tourists: MR = 120 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 25 and P = 70.
- Commuters: MR = 60 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 40.
- Total profit = (70 - 20)(25) + (40 - 20)(20) = 1250 + 400 = 1650.
- The ferry enforces the split by checking commuter passes at the gate.
- Compare with the single-price case in Problem Set 4, Q3. You compute the uniform price yourself. Do not assume it is the average of 70 and 40, and remember that the aggregate demand curve has a kink.

4. The inverse elasticity check (Slide 16)
- Lerner index: (P - MC)/P = -1/Ed, where Ed is the price elasticity of demand at the chosen point.
- Tourists: (70 - 20)/70 = 0.714, so |Ed| = 1.4.
- Commuters: (40 - 20)/40 = 0.5, so |Ed| = 2.
- Prof: "If your Lerner numbers don't match the elasticities you computed from the demand curves, you made an algebra error, not a conceptual one."

5. Welfare - what is on the exam
- Third-degree discrimination can raise or lower total welfare compared with a single price.
- A necessary condition for a welfare gain is that total output rises. The prof calls this "the output test." If output stays the same or falls, welfare cannot have gone up.
- Do NOT write that price discrimination is always inefficient; that answer loses points.
- Second degree: menus are designed so high-value buyers don't pick the low tier. This is the incentive-compatibility constraint. We cover it intuitively only; the formal screening model is taught in ECON 315 and is not on this course's exams.

6. Admin
- Midterm 2: Thursday, Oct 22, in class, 75 minutes. Covers Lectures 6-10.
- Allowed: one handwritten double-sided formula sheet and a non-graphing calculator.
- Office hours moved to Wednesday 3-5 pm, Room HB 211, this week only.
- Problem Set 4 is due Monday before class.
- Next lecture (10): two-part tariffs and the "Disneyland dilemma."

HLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 3410 Lecture 12 notes: Page Replacement and Thrashing
HLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 3410 - Operating Systems
Lecture 12: Page Replacement, Working Sets, and Thrashing
Prof. Emeka Lindqvist. Lecture notes posted by the course staff.

1. The problem
- When memory is full, a page fault forces the kernel to pick a victim frame. How it picks is the page replacement policy.
- Cost model for this course: a hit costs 100 ns; a fault serviced from the SSD costs 80 microseconds.
- Prof: "One fault in a thousand references nearly doubles your effective access time. Faults are not a rounding error."

2. The policies we compare
- OPT (Belady's MIN): evict the page whose next use is furthest in the future. Not implementable; used only as a yardstick.
- FIFO: evict the page that was loaded earliest. Simple, and it suffers from Belady's anomaly.
- LRU: evict the page unused for the longest time. LRU is a stack algorithm, so it never shows Belady's anomaly. Exact LRU needs a timestamp or a list update on every memory reference, which no real MMU provides.
- Clock (second chance): frames sit in a circle with one use bit per frame, set by the hardware whenever the page is referenced. On a fault the hand sweeps: if the use bit is 1, clear it and advance; if it is 0, evict that page. A newly loaded page starts with its use bit set to 1.

3. Slide 9 - Belady's anomaly (FIFO)
- Reference string: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
- With 3 frames: 9 faults. With 4 frames: 10 faults.
- "More memory, more faults" can only happen for policies that are not stack algorithms.

4. Slide 11 - in-class trace (3 frames, all empty at the start)
- Reference string: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3
- Results: FIFO: 9 faults. LRU: 8 faults. Clock: 7 faults.
- Yes, Clock beat LRU on this string. Prof: "Clock approximates LRU on average, not on every string. Don't write that Clock is always worse than LRU."
- Clock trace convention for this course: empty frames are filled in order starting at frame 0; the hand starts at frame 0; after any replacement the hand points to the frame after the one just filled.

5. Working sets and thrashing
- Working set W(t, Delta): the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Delta references. In this course Delta = 10,000 references unless a problem says otherwise.
- Thrashing: the sum of the working set sizes exceeds the number of physical frames, so processes spend more time faulting than running. CPU utilization drops, a naive scheduler admits more processes to use the idle CPU, and things get worse.
- Page fault frequency (PFF): give a process more frames when its fault rate is above an upper bound, take frames away when it is below a lower bound.
- Tern (our teaching kernel, used in Lab 5): the thrash monitor suspends the process with the largest resident set when the system-wide fault rate exceeds 1 fault per 500 references for 3 consecutive sampling windows.

6. Exam notes
- Final exam: you will trace Clock by hand on a new string. Show the use bits and the hand position after every fault.
- Enhanced second chance (use bit plus dirty bit, four classes) was mentioned for context only and is NOT on the final.
- Know why LRU has no Belady's anomaly (the stack property). You do not need the proof.
- Lab 5 is due Friday at 11:59 pm. The autograder checks your thrash monitor against the Tern rule above.

Price discrimination basics
- You need market power, a way to separate buyers, and no resale.

- Second degree: different prices for different groups like students vs seniors.

- Price discrimination is always inefficient compared with a single price, so just write that on the exam.
- Output test: if output goes up, welfare definitely goes up.
- Third degree: less elastic group pays more (this is the one that shows up every year).

ENGINEERING - WHAT THE BLOG SAYS
- "Why we built Harrow" (post by Staff Engineer Maren Dahlquist, 2024): they moved from a single balances table updated in place to a double-entry ledger. Main reasons: they could not explain balance drift to Finance, and refunds were being applied twice when a webhook retried.

- A 2025 postmortem post: the nightly settlement batch overran by about 3 hours one night in November because of lock contention on the payouts table after a big Thanksgiving week. The fix was splitting the batch by grower region and moving to SKIP LOCKED workers. The post ends with "we still don't have good backpressure when volume spikes" - so it is still an open problem.

- On-call was heavy in 2024; he thinks it got better after the Harrow cutover.

- Dockhand's transactional outbox is the same idea as avoiding the double-applied refunds in the Harrow post.
- Sparrowhawk (idempotency keys on PostgreSQL advisory locks) is directly relevant to webhook retries.
- Partitioning load_events by month is relevant to their volume growing from 400k to 1.5M entries per day.

QUESTIONS I WANT TO ASK
1. What does backpressure on the settlement batch look like today, a year after the November overrun?
2. How is the Tallow Terms credit risk modeled in the ledger - separate accounts, or a separate system?
3. What would success look like for this hire in the first 90 days?

- Whether the Pacific Northwest expansion changes the team structure.
- Who the hiring manager is (the recruiter never said).

Req BK-2291: Senior Backend Engineer, Routing Platform
Prepared by Talent Acquisition for recruiter use. Last updated September 15.

Brightkeel builds load-matching and routing software for mid-size freight brokers. The core product, Keelway, matches available truck capacity to open loads and plans multi-stop routes. Routing Platform owns the route planning service, the ETA prediction pipeline, and carrier location ingest. The team is 7 engineers (1 staff, 2 senior, 4 mid-level) plus a shared product manager. The hire reports to Engineering Manager Tomasz Evering. Main stack: Go services, Postgres, Kafka and Redis, deployed on AWS with Terraform. A few legacy Python jobs remain and are being retired this year.

On-call is a 1 week in 7 rotation. Engineers receive a $400 stipend per on-call week. Pages outside business hours averaged about two per week last quarter.

Level and compensation
This is an L5 (Senior) role. Base salary band: $168,000 to $196,000. Equity is granted as stock options with a 4-year vest and a 1-year cliff. Do not share specific equity numbers before the offer stage; tell candidates equity is discussed at offer. Brightkeel can support H-1B transfers for candidates already in H-1B status. We cannot sponsor new cap-subject H-1B petitions for this req.

1. Recruiter screen (30 min)

Promotion cycles run twice a year, in March and September. The path from L5 is to L6 (Staff); the team's current staff engineer was promoted internally last year.

Strong backend fundamentals in a distributed system at production scale. Experience with event-driven pipelines (Kafka or similar), Postgres performance work, and owning services in on-call. Nice to have: routing, geospatial, or logistics domain experience. Frontend experience is not required.

HSEM-CTX-G1.title: Thesis chapter 4 - AMF inoculant and sorghum yield under drought
HSEM-CTX-G1.text:
M.Sc. thesis, Department of Plant Sciences, Halvorsen University
Chapter 4 - Results: Mycorrhizal inoculation and sorghum yield under drought (Kerrow Valley trials)

4.1 Overview
This chapter reports the field results of the three-season trial (2021-2023) that tested whether a commercial arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) inoculant, GlomaSeed-7, improves grain yield of sorghum (cultivar KV-212) under managed drought at the Kerrow Valley research station.

4.2 Design recap
The trial used a randomized complete block design with 4 blocks and a 2 x 2 factorial: inoculation (AMF inoculant vs. sterile carrier control) crossed with water regime (full irrigation vs. managed drought, in which irrigation after flowering was cut to 45% of crop evapotranspiration). Each block contained 12 plots, and each of the four treatment combinations appeared three times per block, giving 48 plots per season. Plots were 6 m x 4 m. The station has a single sandy loam soil series (pH 6.8, available phosphorus 11 mg/kg). Grain was harvested from the central 8 m2 of each plot and adjusted to 13% moisture. Root colonization was scored at flowering with the gridline-intersect method on 5 plants per plot.

4.3 Data loss
In 2022, flooding in late June destroyed 6 plots in block 4, all of them under managed drought. These plots were treated as missing and no values were imputed, so the 2022 analysis uses 42 plots.

4.4 Results
Root colonization at flowering averaged 38% in inoculated plots and 9% in control plots (pooled across seasons).

Under managed drought, inoculated plots yielded on average 11.4% more grain than control plots (pooled means 3.12 t/ha vs. 2.80 t/ha; linear mixed model with season as a random effect, p = 0.004). The drought benefit was largest in 2023 (15.8%) and smallest in 2021 (7.9%); the 2022 figure was 10.6%.

Under full irrigation the difference between inoculated and control plots was 2.1% and not statistically significant (p = 0.27).

The inoculation x water regime interaction was significant (p = 0.018), meaning the effect of the inoculant depended on water supply.

Harvest index did not differ between treatments. Thousand-grain weight was higher with inoculation under drought (27.9 g vs. 26.6 g), which suggests that most of the extra yield came from heavier grain rather than more grains per head.

4.5 Interpretation
A benefit that appears under water stress but not under full irrigation is consistent with the hypothesis that AMF hyphae extend the effective root zone for water and phosphorus uptake as the soil dries. We did not measure hyphal length, leaf water potential or tissue phosphorus, so the mechanism is inferred, not demonstrated.

4.6 Limitations
- Single site and single soil series; the result may not transfer to clay soils or to soils with high available phosphorus.
- One cultivar (KV-212).
- The inoculant cost and economic return were not assessed.
- Native AMF were present in control plots (9% colonization), so the control is better described as "low inoculum" than as "no mycorrhiza".

4.7 Summary
Across three seasons, GlomaSeed-7 raised sorghum grain yield under managed drought by 11.4% on average, with no meaningful effect under full irrigation. The effect is modest, consistent across seasons in direction, and limited in scope to one site, one soil and one cultivar.

HSEM-CTX-G2.title: Study summary - voice assistant latency tolerance in adults 65+
HSEM-CTX-G2.text:
Study summary - Response latency tolerance of voice assistants among adults aged 65 and over
Prepared for the Human-Centred Computing research seminar

Aim
To find out how much delay older adults tolerate between finishing a spoken request and hearing a voice assistant reply, and whether longer delays change behaviour as well as satisfaction.

Participants
62 adults aged 65-84 (median age 72; 34 women, 28 men) were recruited through two community centres in Harlow Bay. Participants who used hearing aids were not excluded, but hearing status was self-reported only and was not tested or used in the analysis.

Design
A within-subjects design was chosen because tolerance for delay varies widely between individuals; with each participant acting as their own baseline, fewer participants were needed to detect a difference. Each participant completed 12 everyday tasks (for example setting a reminder, asking for the weather, adding an item to a shopping list) under each of three latency conditions: 300 ms, 900 ms and 1800 ms. The order of latency conditions was counterbalanced with a Latin square. All sessions took place in a quiet laboratory room at the university, using a prototype smart speaker called Wren. A session lasted about 50 minutes.

Measures
- Satisfaction rated on a 7-point scale after every task.
- Task completion (whether the request was fulfilled without researcher help).
- Re-prompts: the participant repeated or rephrased the request before the reply arrived.
- A short closing interview.

Analysis
Linear mixed-effects models with a random intercept for each participant; pairwise comparisons between latency conditions used Holm correction.

Results
Mean satisfaction was 5.9 at 300 ms, 5.7 at 900 ms and 4.3 at 1800 ms. The difference between 300 ms and 900 ms was not significant (p = 0.41); the drop from 900 ms to 1800 ms was significant (p < 0.001).

Task completion was 94%, 93% and 92% across the three conditions, with no significant difference.

Re-prompts rose sharply at the longest delay: participants repeated the command in 19% of tasks at 1800 ms, compared with 4% at 300 ms. Interviews suggested participants read long silences as the device not having heard them.

In the closing interview, 23 of 62 participants said a short spoken filler such as "one moment" would make waiting easier. Filler cues were not part of the study conditions and were not tested.

Limitations
- Lab setting: a quiet laboratory room, not people's homes.
- English-only tasks and participants.
- A single device (the Wren prototype).
- There was no comparison group of younger adults, so the study cannot say whether older adults are more or less tolerant than other age groups.
- Sessions of about 50 minutes may have introduced some fatigue, although counterbalancing spreads this across conditions.

Conclusion
For this population, delays up to 900 ms did not measurably reduce satisfaction, while 1800 ms did, and it also led people to repeat themselves. A practical design target is to keep response latency at or below about 900 ms. Future work: test spoken filler cues and run an in-home deployment.

HSEM-CTX-G3.title: Seminar slides - Vessford congestion charge and bus ridership
HSEM-CTX-G3.text:
Seminar slides - Did the Vessford congestion charge move people onto buses?
Urban Economics Research Seminar

Slide 1 - Title
Did the Vessford congestion charge move people onto buses? Evidence from an 18-month pilot.

Slide 2 - Question
When a mid-sized city charges cars to enter its centre, how much of the change shows up as extra bus use, and where?

Slide 3 - The policy
From March 2022 Vessford charged 4.50 per car entering the central zone on weekdays between 07:00 and 19:00. The pilot ran for 18 months. Buses, taxis and blue-badge holders were exempt.

Slide 4 - Data
- Fare-card taps on 31 bus routes, aggregated to route-week.
- Camera counts of cars crossing the charging cordon (Vessford only).
- Comparison city: Aldmere, similar population and bus network, no charge.
- 24 months of pre-period data before the charge started.

Slide 5 - Method
Difference-in-differences on a route-week panel: Vessford routes vs. Aldmere routes, before vs. after March 2022. Route fixed effects and week fixed effects. Standard errors clustered by route.

Slide 6 - Parallel trends
Event-study coefficients for the pre-period are all within +/-1.5% and jointly insignificant (p = 0.62). Ridership in the two cities moved together before the charge.

Slide 7 - Main result
- Bus boardings rose 7.2% (95% CI 4.1 to 10.3) relative to Aldmere.
- Car entries into the zone fell 14% compared with the 12 months before the charge. This is a simple before-after comparison from Vessford cordon cameras; Aldmere has no equivalent cordon, so there is no comparison city for this number.

Slide 8 - Where the effect came from
- Routes serving the eastern estates: +11.0%.
- Routes from the northern suburbs: +3.1% (confidence interval crosses zero).
- The eastern estates have the lowest car ownership in the city.

Slide 9 - Robustness
- Placebo start date of March 2021: estimated effect 0.4%, not significant.
- Excluding all December weeks: 6.9%.
- Dropping 2 routes whose timetable frequency changed during 2022: 7.0%.

Slide 10 - What we cannot say
- No air-quality data were collected for the pilot.
- No data on who pays the charge (for example by income), so no distributional analysis yet.
- Fare-card data miss cash fares, which were about 8% of boardings in 2021.
- A new bus lane on Harbour Road opened in May 2022 and affects 3 routes. We cannot fully separate the charge from the bus lane on those routes.

Slide 11 - Conclusions
- The charge is associated with a moderate rise in bus use, concentrated where car ownership is low.
- Most of the fall in car entries is not matched by extra bus boardings; where those trips went is an open question with this data.

Slide 12 - Next steps
- Equity analysis using a household travel survey (fieldwork pending).
- Extend the panel to the full 18 months of cordon data once released.

HSEM-CTX-C1.title: Draft extended abstract - peer-led study groups in first-year chemistry
HSEM-CTX-C1.text:
Extended abstract (draft) - Peer-led study groups and first-year chemistry outcomes
Education Research Seminar

Abstract
We report a randomized study of peer-led study groups in first-year general chemistry during the autumn 2023 semester. 241 students took part. Students in peer-led groups had a pass rate 9 percentage points higher than students without groups, and we conclude that peer-led study groups improve first-year chemistry outcomes.

Methods
The course enrolled 530 students. In week 2, all students were offered a place in a weekly peer-led study group run by second-year students; 214 students chose to join a group and attended at least 6 of 10 sessions. The comparison group was the remaining students who did not join. Because students self-selected into groups, we adjusted for prior high-school chemistry grade and for attendance at lectures. Data come from the spring 2024 semester records supplied by the registry.

Results
Pass rate (final grade C or above): study-group students 71%, comparison students 65%. After adjustment for prior grade and lecture attendance the difference remained positive. Mean final exam score was 64.2 for study-group students and 61.8 for the comparison group.

Discussion
Peer-led groups appear to be associated with better outcomes. Students who join voluntary groups may differ in motivation from students who do not, and this was not measured directly. Attendance at the groups fell over the term, from an average of 19 students per session in week 3 to 11 in week 10, and the students who stayed longest may be the most motivated. Peer leaders received four hours of training before the semester. We plan to repeat the study next year with a waiting-list design so that group places can be allocated by lottery.
HSEM-CTX-C1.notes: Contradictions: abstract says "randomized" but methods say students self-selected (214 chose to join); abstract says 241 students vs 214 in methods; abstract claims +9 percentage points but results give 71% vs 65% (6 points); study period autumn 2023 in abstract vs spring 2024 registry records in methods; abstract states causal "improve" while discussion only says "associated".

HTECH-CTX-G1.title: Tallowmarket Go coding session pre-read: Escrow Hold Overlap
HTECH-CTX-G1.text:
TALLOWMARKET - GO CODING SESSION PRE-READ
Problem: Escrow Hold Overlap (version 2)

Background
When a restaurant places an order, Tallowmarket places an escrow hold on the funds until the grower confirms delivery. Our Risk team wants to know how many holds are open at the same time, because the banking partner charges a fee tier based on the peak number of simultaneous holds in a day.

Part A (required)
You are given n holds. Each hold has an id, a start minute and an end minute. A hold covers the half-open interval [start, end): it is active at minute start and no longer active at minute end. Two holds that touch (one ends at 40, the other starts at 40) do not overlap.
Return two integers: the maximum number of holds active at the same instant, and the earliest instant at which that maximum is reached. If n is 0, return "0 -1".

Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 200,000
- 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000,000 (integers, minutes since the start of the settlement epoch)
- Holds are NOT sorted. Ids are unique strings of up to 12 characters.
- Target: O(n log n) time. Your solution runs with a 2 second limit and 256 MB of memory.

Example 1
Input:
H1 10 50
H2 20 40
H3 40 70
H4 45 60
H5 70 90
Output: 3 45
Explanation: at minute 45, H1, H3 and H4 are active. At minute 40, H2 has already ended, so only H1 and H3 are active there.

Example 2
Input:
H1 5 15
H2 15 25
H3 25 35
Output: 1 5

Example 3
Input: (no holds)
Output: 0 -1

Part B (required)
Each hold also carries amount_cents, a positive integer up to 50,000,000. Return the maximum total amount_cents held at the same instant and the earliest instant it is reached. Use a 64-bit integer; the sum can exceed 2^31.

Example 4
Input:
H1 0 30 5000
H2 10 20 9000
H3 20 40 7000
Output: 14000 10
Explanation: during [10, 20) H1 and H2 are both held, 14000 in total. At minute 20, H2 ends and H3 starts, so the total drops to H1 + H3 = 12000.

Part C (discussion only, no code)
Holds will eventually arrive as a stream from Kafka, up to 50,000 inserts per second at peak, and a hold may also be cancelled before its end minute. Describe how you would keep the Part A answer current after each insert or cancel. We care about the data structure and its complexity, not a full implementation.

What we look at
- Correct handling of touching intervals. This is the most common mistake we see.
- Tie-breaking: when the maximum is reached more than once, report the earliest instant.
- Clear naming and small functions. Standard library only; no third-party packages.
- A few table-driven tests.

Please do not share this problem publicly. Questions about the statement can be raised with the session interviewer at the start of the call.

HTECH-CTX-G2.title: Dockhand design summary v1.3 (candidate project)
HTECH-CTX-G2.text:
DOCKHAND - Design Summary (v1.3)
Author: Tobias Venkataraman | Larkspur Freight, Platform Backend | Last updated: 2024-11-18
Status: in production since June 2024

1. Purpose
Dockhand moves shipment status events (picked up, in transit, delayed, delivered, exception) from the services that record them into Kafka, so that billing, the customer portal and the carrier-settlement services from Project Tern can react without polling the database. Volume is about 2.3 million events per day on average, with a morning peak of roughly 410 events per second between 07:30 and 09:00 Eastern.

2. Why an outbox
Before Dockhand, services wrote to PostgreSQL and then published to Kafka in the same request. When the publish failed after the commit, the event was lost; when the commit failed after the publish, consumers saw an event for a change that never happened. Dockhand uses a transactional outbox: the service writes the business row and an outbox row in the same PostgreSQL transaction. Nothing is published inside the request.

3. Components
- outbox_events table: one row per event (event_id UUID, shipment_id, event_type, payload JSONB, created_at, published_at). Partitioned by day; partitions older than 72 hours are dropped by a scheduled job, which is cheaper than DELETE plus vacuum.
- Relay: a Go service that polls unpublished rows every 250 ms in batches of up to 500, ordered by created_at, publishes them, then sets published_at. Two relay instances run, but only one is active at a time: the active one holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock. If it dies, the standby acquires the lock; failover has taken up to 30 seconds in drills.
- Topic shipment-status.v2: 24 partitions, keyed by shipment_id, replication factor 3, producer acks=all.
- Consumers: each consumer records processed event_id values in a dedupe table (processed_events) inside the same transaction as its own side effects. Entries are kept for 7 days.
- Dead-letter topic shipment-status.dlq: a message goes there after 5 failed attempts with exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds.

4. Delivery guarantees
Dockhand is at-least-once, not exactly-once. The relay can publish a batch and crash before it sets published_at; on restart that batch is published again. Duplicates are expected and are removed by the consumer-side dedupe on event_id. Ordering is guaranteed per shipment only (same key, same partition). There is no ordering across shipments.

5. Service levels
Target: p99 time from outbox commit to consumer receipt under 4 seconds. Measured in October 2024: p50 0.6 s, p99 2.9 s, excluding relay failovers.

6. Alternatives considered
- Debezium change data capture: rejected for v1 because the platform team did not run Kafka Connect yet, and we did not want to own a Connect cluster for one pipeline. Revisit in 2025.
- Publishing directly from the request with retries: rejected; it cannot close the gap between commit and publish.
- SQS FIFO: rejected because the billing and settlement teams already consumed from Kafka, and FIFO throughput limits per message group would have needed careful sharding.

7. Known limitations
- The single active relay is a throughput ceiling; load tests showed it saturates near 3,000 events per second.
- JSON payloads carry a schema_version field, but there is no schema registry; breaking changes are coordinated by hand.
- The dedupe window is 7 days, so replaying older messages from the DLQ requires a manual override flag.

8. Open questions
- Whether to move the relay to logical replication once Kafka Connect exists.
- Whether 24 partitions is enough if the Tern consumers need more parallelism.
